paragraphs: My last paper gave several reasons why union would best protect the safety of the people against the danger of JUST causes of war given to other nations. Those reasons show that a national government would give such causes more rarely, and would also settle them more easily, than either the State governments or the proposed little confederacies could.

But the safety of the people of America against dangers from FOREIGN force depends on more than their avoiding just causes of war. It also depends on their placing and keeping themselves in a position that does not INVITE hostility or insult. I hardly need point out that there are PRETENDED causes of war as well as just ones.

It is only too true, however shameful to human nature, that nations in general will make war whenever they see something to gain by it. Absolute monarchs will even make war when their nations stand to gain nothing, for purely personal ends: a thirst for military glory, revenge for a personal insult, ambition, or private agreements to enrich or support their own families or partisans. These motives and many others touch only the mind of the sovereign, and they often lead him into wars that justice does not sanction and his people neither want nor benefit from. These inducements are more common in absolute monarchies, but they deserve our attention. Apart from them, however, there are others that move nations as often as kings, and some of them, as we shall see, grow out of our own situation and circumstances.

We are rivals of France and Britain in the fisheries. We can supply their markets more cheaply than they can supply themselves, whatever they do to prevent it with bounties on their own fish or duties on foreign fish.

We are rivals of those two and of most other European nations in navigation and the carrying trade. We deceive ourselves if we suppose that any of them will be glad to see that trade flourish. Our carrying trade cannot grow without taking something from theirs, so it is in their interest, and will be their policy, to hold it back rather than help it.

In the trade to China and India we compete with more than one nation. That trade lets us share advantages they had almost monopolized, and it lets us supply ourselves with goods we used to buy from them.

Any nation that holds territory on or near this continent will be displeased to see our commerce expand in our own ships. The cheapness and excellence of our products, our closeness, and the enterprise and skill of our merchants and sailors will give us a larger share of what those territories offer than their sovereigns wish or find consistent with their policy.

Spain finds it convenient to shut the Mississippi to us on one side, and Britain shuts us out of the Saint Lawrence on the other. Neither will allow the other waters that lie between them and us to become channels of mutual contact and trade.

The people of America know that inducements to war may arise from these circumstances, as well as from others not so obvious at present. They know too that, whenever those inducements find a fit time and opportunity to act, pretenses to color and justify them will not be lacking. They are therefore wise to regard union and a good national government as necessary to put and keep them in SUCH A SITUATION that war is discouraged and held down instead of being INVITED. That situation consists in the best possible state of defense, and it depends necessarily on the government, the arms, and the resources of the country.

The safety of the whole is the interest of the whole, and it cannot be provided for without government, whether one government, a few, or many. Let us ask, then, whether one good government is not better equipped for this purpose than any other number.

One government can gather and use the talents and experience of the ablest men, wherever in the Union they may be found. It can act on uniform principles of policy. It can bring the several parts and members into harmony, make them alike, and protect them, and it can extend the benefit of its foresight and precautions to each. In making treaties, it will look to the interest of the whole, and to the particular interests of the parts as bound up with that of the whole. It can bring the resources and power of the whole to the defense of any one part, and it can do so more easily and quickly than State governments or separate confederacies, which lack concert and unity of system. It can put the militia under one plan of discipline and place their officers in a proper line of subordination to the chief executive. In effect it will thus join them into one corps, and make them more effective than if they were split into thirteen, or three or four, distinct and independent companies.

What would the militia of Britain amount to if the English militia took orders from the government of England, the Scottish militia from the government of Scotland, and the Welsh militia from the government of Wales? Suppose an invasion. Would those three governments, if they agreed at all, be able to act against the enemy with all their forces as effectively as the single government of Great Britain?

We have heard much about the fleets of Britain, and the time may come, if we are wise, when the fleets of America will draw attention. But suppose one national government had not regulated British navigation so as to make it a nursery for seamen. Suppose one national government had not called forth all the national means and materials for building fleets. Then British prowess and British thunder would never have been celebrated. Let England have its navigation and fleet, and Scotland its own, and Wales its own, and Ireland its own. Let those four constituent parts of the British empire live under four independent governments, and it is easy to see how soon each would shrink into comparative insignificance.

Apply these facts to our own case. Suppose America left divided into thirteen independent governments, or, if you like, three or four. What armies could they raise and pay? What fleets could they ever hope to have? If one were attacked, would the others rush to its aid and spend their blood and money in its defense? Would there be no danger that they would be flattered into neutrality by its attractive promises? Or that they would be seduced by too great a love of peace into refusing to risk their tranquillity and present safety for the sake of neighbors whom they have perhaps been jealous of, and whose importance they are content to see reduced? Such conduct would not be wise, but it would be natural. The history of the states of Greece, and of other countries, is full of such instances, and it is not unlikely that what has so often happened would happen again in similar circumstances.

But suppose they were willing to help the invaded State or confederacy. How, when, and in what proportion should they send men and money? Who would command the allied armies, and from which of the allies would he take his orders? Who would settle the terms of peace, and, if disputes arose, what umpire would decide between them and force them to comply? Such a situation would bring endless difficulties and problems. One government, in contrast, would watch over the general and common interests and would combine and direct the powers and resources of the whole. It would be free of all these embarrassments, and it would do far more for the safety of the people.

But whatever our situation may be, whether firmly united under one national government or split into a number of confederacies, foreign nations will certainly see it exactly as it is and will treat us accordingly. Suppose they see an effective and well-administered national government, a prudently regulated trade, a properly organized and disciplined militia, carefully managed resources and finances, restored credit, and a people free, contented, and united. They will then be much more inclined to seek our friendship than to provoke our resentment. Suppose, on the other hand, they find us without an effective government, with each State doing right or wrong as its rulers find convenient. Or suppose they find us split into three or four independent and probably quarreling republics or confederacies, one leaning to Britain, another to France, and a third to Spain, and perhaps played against one another by the three. What a poor, pitiful figure America will make in their eyes! How exposed she would be, not only to their contempt but to their outrage! And how soon dearly bought experience would proclaim that when a people or a family divides in this way, it never fails to divide against itself.
